item.title: Exclusive: Secret pay-for-play text rocks Trump White House
item.description:
Top Trump adviser Ric Grenell allegedly outlined a stunning pay-for-influence offer to a Turkish billionaire last year: access to "POTUS," "VIP events" and administration officials, according to a text message, reviewed by Axios, that the White House counsel is investigating.

  • "Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you'll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS," the May 3, 2025, text says.
  • Grenell has called the accusations "lies" and denied sending the text message.

Why it matters: Administration officials say the text is a key piece of evidence in the White House's investigation — ordered by President Trump — into whether Grenell abused the president's trust and misappropriated a potential multimillion-dollar donation to the Kennedy Center, which Grenell led at the time.

  • Grenell also served in another Trump-appointed capacity: as special envoy to Venezuela, where Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon also had contracts.
  • "We need to make you the 'American face' down in V," Grenell allegedly wrote in the same 2025 text message to Mildon, whose attorneys sent the text, at least one financial document and other correspondence to the White House counsel's office, according to sources familiar with the investigation.
  • Mildon is married to another Trump adviser: former U.S. attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba, who stormed into the Oval Office on Oct. 9 and accused Grenell of hoodwinking her husband into making a Kennedy Center donation that never arrived, Axios first reported.

Zoom in: At the heart of the alleged scheme is a financial transaction involving a private Houston-based defense company's software and the Democratic Republic of Congo, Habba and Mildon's attorneys have told the White House.

  • Mildon alleges that at Grenell's direction, Mildon wired $17.6 million to Texas Armament & Technology. He says the money was to be split in roughly two parts: one for the Congo deal and nearly $6 million for the Kennedy Center.
  • To back up his claims, Mildon provided the 2025 text that discussed the Kennedy Center donation and Congo "software." In the text to Mildon, the sender also says, "There is an e-mail that was sent to you, can you please take a look at it for me ?"
  • That email also was furnished to the White House, as was a May 29, 2025, financial record showing $17.6 million was wired to the company, known by its initials TXAT, sources said.

It would be 17 months before Mildon learned that the Kennedy Center never received the money that he thought was included in the wire he sent at Grenell's direction, Habba told the president.

The intrigue: Here's where the story gets mysterious and murky. It's unclear what the Congo contract was for, how it related to the Kennedy Center or what the financial specifics were.

  • The text doesn't mention any financial numbers, either for TXAT or the Kennedy Center. But a source familiar with the situation said that other correspondence furnished to the White House does have financial specifics.
  • The financial transaction sent to TXAT didn't appear to come from Mildon's bank account, as Habba initially indicated to Trump.

Instead, the $17.6 million was wired to TXAT from Congo's "Ministère des Finances" in Kinshasa, the capital city, where Mildon has business and access to finances, a White House official said.

  • A spokesman for Mildon would not comment. Spokespeople for TXAT and Congo's government couldn't be reached.
  • "We're trying to find out whose money this is," the official said.

Complicating the matter further: Habba's numbers kept changing after she first alerted Trump to the alleged theft of the Kennedy Center money.

  • At first she said the Kennedy Center contribution was for $17 million.
  • Then she said it was about $6 million after talking to Mildon. The exact figure seems to be $5.6 million.

The other side: Grenell, who declined to comment for this article, previously told Axios that the claims against him are "absurd."

  • "I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all," he said. "Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations."
  • When told of the text message's exact wording, Grenell hotly denied he sent it because "center" was spelled in British English as "centre," a source briefed on his thinking said.
  • Grenell's allies also have questioned everything from Mildon's background as a businessman to his associates, his age (he's 29 but some records indicate he's 25) and his $10 million wedding last month to Habba, 42, whom he began dating last year.

Friction point: As the New York Times examined Mildon's activities in Venezuela, he had a falling out with Grenell, with whom he had been friendly since 2024.

  • Mildon met Habba in 2025 at the Kennedy Center.

Inside the room: On Oct. 9, when Habba arrived at the White House, she was "pretty animated," said one administration official, and exclaimed at one point, "Ric stole the money!"

  • The problem, however, was that Habba "didn't have all her stuff in order. She went in there half-cocked without all the facts yelling about Grenell stealing. And the facts keep changing," the source said. "That doesn't mean Ric is out of the woods. This looks really shady."
  • After Habba leveled her accusations, Trump called White House Counsel Will Scharf into Oval Office and asked him to look into her claims, sources said.

Trump and Scharf then phoned Grenell, who denied everything and said he would have instantly alerted everyone to the idea of a $17 million contribution.

  • "There's no way this is true. This is crazy," Grenell told Trump at one point, according to a source briefed on the discussion.

Behind the scenes: Scharf grew skeptical of Habba's claims early last week because she and Mildon's attorneys were initially slow to furnish any records to help his inquiry, said a source. They submitted the documents on Friday.

  • Scharf is still gathering evidence and plans to verify the digital footprint of the 2025 text, the source said, noting that a printout of the message has the same image of Grenell that appears on his smartphone contact card display.
  • Kennedy Center insiders also have contacted the White House and said they frequently saw Mildon at exclusive events at the facility, indicating he was a big donor. That includes appearances in the vice president's box, next to the president's, a source said.
  • "Here's where Alina might be telling the truth: Mildon did get access. So why did he get access? Was he doing business in Congo with Ric? Why so much access if the contribution was never paid?" one of the administration officials asked.
  • "There's a lot of questions. And POTUS wants answers."

item.title: Supreme Court won't revive accused 9/11 mastermind's plea deal
item.description:
The Supreme Court denied on Monday a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind behind the 9/11 terror attacks, to reinstate plea agreements that would have spared him and two co-defendants the death penalty.

Why it matters: The denial keeps the death penalty on the table for the accused 9/11 plotters as they move closer to their June 2028 military trial date, when the government hopes to finally secure convictions more than 25 years after one of America's deadliest terrorist attacks.

Driving the news: The Supreme Court released an order list Monday identifying the cases it intends to hear and denying those it won't, like the petition in Khalid Shaikh Mohammad, et al. v. United States.

  • The order doesn't explain why the appeal was rejected.
  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from the decision. He served as associate counsel to President George W. Bush, where he reportedly assisted with legal and policy discussions following 9/11.

Catch up quick: The government and the three men entered into plea agreements in 2024 that would have spared them the death penalty.

  • The decision was met with outrage and pushback from some 9/11 victims' families.
  • Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin withdrew the agreements days later, declaring that "responsibility for such a decision should rest with me."
  • Mohammed and his co-defendants, Walid bin 'Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, appealed that decision. While a military court initially sided with the defendants, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit sided with Austin, prompting their final appeal to the Supreme Court .

Zoom out: Mohammed and his co-defendants were first arraigned in 2008 for their alleged roles in the attacks involving four hijacked planes that struck the Twin Towers in New York City and the Pentagon, with a fourth crashing in Pennsylvania.

  • Mohammed and his fellow defendants have been held at the U.S. military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
  • Prosecutors had sought a January 2027 trial date, but a judge determined that timeline would leave too little time to resolve outstanding pretrial issues.

What we're watching: The new tentative trial date is for June 5, 2028. Go deeper: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to stand trial in 2028 over 9/11 attacks

item.title: The fallout from Trump's Russia energy moves
item.description:
President Trump's moves to avoid new penalties on Russian energy sent shockwaves through Washington, sparking diplomatic tensions and political turmoil.

Why it matters: Trump's push to lower energy prices ahead of the midterms could provide Russia an economic lifeline and is exposing divisions within his own party.

  • Oil, gas and petroleum product exports help finance Russia's war on Ukraine.

Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month.

  • That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans.

Here's what's on our radar:

A new rationale. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in CNN and ABC appearances yesterday, called the diesel deal a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine.

  • It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week."
  • Ukrainian drone strikes have lowered Russia's refining capacity. Trump, in a Truth Social post yesterday, also cast his recent decisions as a way to get a peace deal with Russia.

A new clock. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Saturday that Trump wants to take 60 days to review implementing the Graham Act in order to gauge its impact on the global and U.S. economies.

A deteriorating relationship. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has sharply and publicly criticized both the diesel deal and Trump's decision to waive, for now, the Graham Act penalties.

  • Trump's post, meanwhile, bashed Zelensky for hitting Russian refineries, "knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States."

Republican rifts. Many GOP lawmakers and candidates, to varying degrees, have joined Democrats in criticizing Trump's Friday night sanctions waivers and the diesel deal days earlier.

  • Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision not to implement, for now, the bipartisan law named after her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).
  • She's running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother. Former Rep. Mike Rogers — the GOP candidate in Michigan's tight Senate race — also expressed concern with the decision but avoided directly criticizing Trump on CNN yesterday.
  • Other Republicans were far harsher, including retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who called Friday night's move "beyond irresponsible."

Lame duck rumblings. "A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they're ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia," The Hill reports.

What we're watching: With the midterms just weeks away, more Republicans are openly breaking with Trump.

item.title: Bob Woodward reveals "dream source" in memoir, "Secrets," out next month
item.description:
Bob Woodward — in an eye-opening excerpt from his forthcoming memoir, "Secrets," that's previewed in the new issue of The New Yorker — reveals that one of his best friends, the late Richard Darman, was also one of his best sources during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations.

  • "Darman was willing, even eager at times, to talk about the most sensitive intelligence matters, including N.S.A. intercepts and covert C.I.A. operations," Woodward writes in his book, out Nov. 15. "He was always careful not to talk about matters that would harm national security, I believed, but he would go right up to the edge — a reporter's dream source."

Why it matters: Woodward, 83 — who followed the blockbuster Watergate reporting of his youth with a shelf of revelatory books about American presidents — gives a searingly honest account of the collapse of his friendship with Darman after a Post series that was damaging to Bush. Woodward details a disappointment in his Washington Post career and, in the case of a story where he was the responsible editor, a "moral failing."

  • The New Yorker calls the Darman excerpt "A Dangerous Friendship," revealing the danger of "getting too close to a source." Woodward and Darman never reconciled, although "Secrets" describes their deathbed encounter.

Woodward writes in his New Yorker debut that he and Darman, who controlled the paper flow to Reagan as staff secretary and was budget director for Bush 41, "had countless long lunches together — Saturday or Sunday — at the Madison Hotel, across the street from the Post, discussing government, journalism, and ourselves":

"I felt like I was getting a master class in how government really operated. Plus, many scoops. In later years, Darman would drive out on weekends to our country house near Annapolis, Maryland, to spend large parts of the day with me and my wife, the journalist Elsa Walsh, who was particularly fond of him. Some people found him arrogant, but I loved his comfortable confidence as a friend and a source. It was part of what made him so extraordinary and valuable. He knew how to turn on the charm, and he did for both Elsa and me."

Behind the scenes: "From critical national-security information to the colorful office tales he shared, Darman provided me with a gold mine of information," Woodward recalls. "I interviewed him in at least fifty-eight meetings or phone conversations. I have boxes filled with hundreds of pages of notes on our discussions. After our most important conversations, as is my practice, I typed a memo of one to six pages, laying out in detail what he'd said."

  • Detailing Darman's "hatchet man" role, Woodward reveals that the "hardest of Darman's targets to dislodge was the First Lady, Nancy Reagan. While Darman poured scorn on her in private, describing her to me as a 'mean bitch,' he could not find a way to drive a stake into her heart."

After a hard-won legislative victory, Darman told Woodward, Reagan said: "Whew! Ever feel like you shit a pineapple?"

  • Keep reading ... Get "Secrets."

item.title: Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America
item.description:
Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year.

Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift.

What they're saying: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday.

  • He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant.
  • He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens.

By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S.

  • If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion.
  • Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings.

Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX.

  • In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts, a gift now worth nearly $300 million.

Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more.

  • Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with background details.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year.

Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift.

What they're saying: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday.

  • He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant.
  • He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens.

By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S.

  • If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion.
  • Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings.

Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX.

  • In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts, a gift now worth nearly $300 million.

Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more.

  • Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with background details.

item.title: How AI giants will reshape global philanthropy
item.description:
The AI boom is about to rewrite the rules of global philanthropy, shifting its center of gravity to Silicon Valley, where the IPOs of AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI will create the world's largest charitable organizations.

Why it matters: Rather than massive donations earmarked for renaming hospital wings or university graduate programs, expect the new wave of giving to mirror startup culture: flexible capital, ambitious bets and a search for measurable impact.

Driving the news: Anthropic announced Sunday that it plans to launch a massive benefit fund with 5% of its shares.

Zoom in: The company's pledge — which would amount to $100 billion if it reaches a value of $2 trillion in its IPO — will go to a public benefit fund and is set to grow as its valuation rises.

  • Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned LLC, giving it flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or distribute money directly to specific populations.
  • The commitment builds on the pledges of co-founders to give away 80% of their equity. A program available to early Anthropic hires and used by a large number of company staffers matched donations at a 3:1 ratio. The company says roughly half its employees participate in donation matching.
  • The company says the fund's shares will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or abroad.

The big picture: Anthropic is joining OpenAI, which is controlled by a nonprofit foundation that holds a 26% equity stake in the company, worth about $130 billion based on the company's current valuation. The foundation has the power to appoint OpenAI's board.

What they're saying: Anthropic says much of its public-benefit work — including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research and discounts for nonprofits and scientific institutions — will continue inside the company.

  • The new fund is intended to make other kinds of giving possible at greater scale, the company says.
  • Anthropic cited AI's effects on the labor market as one potential use and said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue, but that "bolder approaches may be needed."
  • Anthropic has not specified what those approaches would be, or whether the fund would make direct payments to workers affected by AI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's founders and some employees have close ties to effective altruism, a movement ostensibly dedicated to directing resources toward causes where they may do the most good.

  • Effective altruism has come under sharp criticism from the Trump White House, which has emphasized aspects of the movement that are far from the philanthropic mainstream.
  • Those include an acute interest in animal welfare, as well as seemingly abstract ponderings about the value of life, including comparing that of an infant to an adult, or future people to present people.
  • In an X post, Taylor Budowich, a former White House official, highlighted one such comment from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2010, when he said in a blog post that an adult death is "perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant's death."
  • Budowich also shared a few other "insane beliefs of those who make up Anthropic and how they think about prioritizing charitable giving."

The bottom line: Anthropic's fund — and the charitable giving of a massive new cadre of millionaires and deca-millionaires — could become one of the largest vehicles for new giving.

  • The bigger change may come with a new generation of Silicon Valley donors aiming to reset the agenda of modern philanthropy.

item.title: The AI attack-ad nightmare is coming true
item.description:
AI is producing reality-bending midterm ads about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a "Death to America" playing card.

Why it matters: The warnings about deepfakes are coming true. Election laws haven't kept pace with a world where campaigns can put words in opponents' mouths and create realistic-looking scenes that didn't happen.

  • The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans.
  • Four states have laws prohibiting certain uses of AI-generated deepfakes in political ads, while 27 more require some form of disclosure about their use.
  • No federal law specifically regulates AI-generated political ads.

The big picture: An Axios analysis found numerous political ads partly or fully made by generative AI, sometimes undisclosed.

Georgia Senate: Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, has run a series of AI-generated deepfake ads depicting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff getting beauty treatments.

  • The ads mock Ossoff's reported campaign spending on hair and makeup, saying he "talks pretty" but has "an ugly record" and "a lot to cover up."
  • Ossoff said in a C-SPAN interview: "It is deeply troubling to see ... deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising. And it's a slippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate, and the ad should come down immediately."
  • The ads don't disclose AI use, which Georgia law doesn't require.

Michigan Senate: A super PAC called Front Line Action used AI in an ad depicting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo with podcaster Hasan Piker and four women wearing niqabs.

  • Another AI-generated scene has El-Sayed playing a Risk-style board game with his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, and Piker. It depicts cards bearing statements that include "Death to America," "Do not Celebrate Thanksgiving" and "Celebrate 9/11."
  • The group has defended the ad, telling CNN it is "grounded in El-Sayed's own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign."
  • The ad features both a written and spoken disclosure that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence."

New York governor: Republican Bruce Blakeman's campaign and allied super PACs have repeatedly used generative AI in ads attacking Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, with varying degrees of disclosure.

  • One AI-generated ad released by the Blakeman campaign depicts the Tooth Fairy struggling to come up with cash to give to children, saying she "just can't afford to be the Tooth Fairy in Kathy Hochul's New York."
  • Another Blakesman spot says onscreen: "We asked AI what a truthful Kathy Hochul ad would look like." The ad features AI-generated scenes of Hochul attending an upscale dinner and standing outside a police precinct while a man asks her: "Want some crack?"

Pennsylvania governor: A new ad from Republican candidate Stacy Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro talking about taxes, abortion and data centers.

  • The spot puts this quote in his mouth: "This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers. Fact is, I was the one who fast-tracked data centers right here in PA, right after they handed me $5 million in political contributions."
  • Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder, in a statement to Axios, dismissed the ad as "cheap, dishonest AI bullshit."

Texas Senate: Democratic candidate James Talarico has been a consistent target of AI-generated ads from both Republican Ken Paxton's campaign and outside super PACs.

  • A Paxton campaign ad uses AI to depict Talarico defacing a Bible with crayon and saying, "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were."
  • Talarico told NBC he "tried in the legislature to ban AI deepfake videos in political campaigns because they are misleading. They are lying about a candidate in this race."

Kentucky's 6th District: No Going Back PAC, backed by President Trump's MAGA Inc., has run several ads using AI to boost Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado.

  • One ad features multiple AI-generated deepfakes of Democrat Zach Dembo, including one scene in which he stares into the camera.
  • "I expected them to lie about my record, but I did not expect them to lie about my appearance," Dembo said in a statement to Axios, adding that "using AI to create fake or misleading images is the beginning of a very dangerous path for our democracy."

item.title: Rivals pile on Beshear over his resistance to Latinos' push for Texas funds
item.description:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is in open war with prominent Latino lawmakers, and his potential 2028 rivals for president are taking advantage.

  • Beshear, as head of the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), has resisted pressure from Latino leaders to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor, opting to focus on races in other states.
  • In response, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore have given money to Hinojosa's bid to unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) — and earned praise from Latino lawmakers.

Why it matters: The back-and-forth amounts to one of the first fights of the 2028 Democratic primary, against the backdrop of the party's desperation to reverse the GOP's recent gains among Latino voters.

  • Latino leaders are trying to flex their political muscle, fueled in part by Democrats' new primary schedule, which has Nevada and New Mexico — and their large Latino populations — the second and fourth states to vote in the nominating contest.

Driving the news: In recent weeks Latino leaders have gone public in their pressure campaign to push Beshear to invest $10 million in Texas, as polls have shown Hinojosa ahead or within the polls' margin of error.

  • Beshear, mindful of how expensive it is to campaign statewide in Texas and the DGA's limited resources, resisted and instead focused the committee's resources on governor's races in critical states like Nevada, Georgia, Arizona, Wisconsin and Ohio.

Pritzker, a potential 2028 rival to Beshear who already had donated $200,000 to Hinojosa's campaign, then publicly announced he was donating an additional $1 million to Hinojosa. That won the Illinois governor, a billionaire who has strategically spread some of his personal wealth across the party, some fans.

  • "When Latino leaders asked for the cavalry, JB Pritzker sent it, putting $1.2 million behind Gina Hinojosa because he knows the race is winnable," Cristóbal Alex, board chair of the Latino Victory Fund, told Axios.
  • Alex noted that Pritzker, who hosted a fundraiser for the Latino Victory Fund, has "put his resources and his time into Hispanic candidates and voters around the country."

Newsom, meanwhile, sent a fundraising email that brought in $75,000 for Hinojosa.

  • Moore privately told the DGA to reallocate $100,000 from his reelection campaign to Texas, two Democratic officials told Axios.
  • Beshear, who personally donated $25,000 to Hinojosa's campaign, ultimately announced the DGA would give her team $1 million — 10% of the original ask and a small commitment for a big state like Texas. The money arrived this past week, according to a source familiar with the situation.

The intrigue: Several Latino leaders and lawmakers were furious that Beshear didn't attend a Zoom call with them and the DGA on Oct. 7 to discuss the Texas race.

  • "It just baffles me that someone who was even thinking of 2028 would disrespect us and not meet," Rep. Silvia Garcia (D-Texas) told Axios, noting that seven Latino members of Congress were on the call. "Just freaking five minutes on a Zoom … and excuse yourself."
  • "I really felt like he disrespected the group, and that he is going to have a serious Latino problem if he doesn't know how to do the outreach and the communication that's going to need to get us to the White House."
  • Beshear's critics note he had time this fall for a book tour when, they argue, he could have been raising more money for the DGA.

The other side: Several Democrats told Axios that they believe the DGA made the right strategic decision to send money to other states.

  • Some of the Latino leaders pressuring Beshear also were consultants who stood to make money if he invested heavily in Texas.
  • Many Latino leaders claim they speak for Latino voters, but have been proved wrong in recent elections, as Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and others have pointed out.
  • Nevada, Georgia, Wisconsin, and Arizona are swing states likely to be more critical than Texas for a Democrat to get 270 Electoral College votes in 2028.

What they're saying: DGA communications director Sam Newton told Axios: "Unfortunately for the D.C. staffers who are personally obsessed with 2028 and manufacturing Democratic infighting, the DGA and our chair Gov. Beshear, along with all of our Democratic governors, remain solely focused on beating Trump and Republicans to win as many of our high-stakes 36 races for governor as possible."

  • A person familiar with conversation within the DGA conversations told CNN that their internal polls had Hinojosa trailing Abbott by 5 points, but Hinojosa's campaign this week released an internal poll showing her up by 2.
  • The DGA didn't respond to questions about the discrepancy and pointed Axios to its promotion of the poll showing Hinojosa up by 2.

The bottom line: Even some Democrats who think the DGA made the right financial decision not to invest heavily in Texas think Beshear mishandled the politics of the situation.

  • If he can't handle the politics of being DGA chair, they argue, how could he handle a presidential campaign, and potentially the White House?

item.title: Zelensky speaks to Witkoff and Kushner amid U.S.-Ukraine crisis
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke Sunday with President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the crisis between the countries and U.S. efforts to resume peace talks with Russia.

Why it matters: It was the first call between Zelensky and senior U.S. officials since tensions spiked between their countries after Trump cut a diesel deal with Russia 10 days ago.

  • During the call that lasted around 40 minutes, Zelensky discussed with Trump's envoy the possibility of holding an in-person meeting in the coming days.

The latest: Trump defended his decision to grant a waiver related to sanctions pushed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), saying he didn't want to jeopardize negotiations with Russia.

  • "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
  • Trump also accused Zelensky of targeting Russian diesel refineries and not wanting to end the war.

Driving the news: The call took place amid assertions by Zelensky that the Trump administration was behind restrictions imposed on the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military.

  • "Who made this decision? I don't know. I think that this is really both [a White House and SpaceX] decision. If President Trump will decide tomorrow, or better today, if he will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before," Zelensky said on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday.
  • He added, "The message came from [the U.S.] government. I don't know from whom. It's the opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course also my opinion, that it was a message from the American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it."
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the U.S. government was not involved in the Starlink restrictions and said it has been restored. Ukrainian officials dispute that.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

item.title: 95% of MAGA Republicans approve of Trump. For non-MAGA Republicans, it's 47%.
item.description:
Three national polls show President Trump's approval rating hitting new lows as Democrats lead Republicans by 8 to 10 points ahead of the midterms.

Why it matters: Republicans need Trump's loyalists to turn out, but embracing an unpopular president risks alienating independents they need to win competitive races.

Driving the news: New polls from the Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos, NBC News and Fox News put Trump's approval at 33%, 34% and 36%, respectively — record or second-term lows in each survey.

  • Democrats lead Republicans by eight points in the Post poll, nine points in Fox's and 10 points in NBC's among registered voters.
  • Once a strength, the economy is now Trump's main vulnerability. Just 21% approve of his handling of the cost of living in the Post poll, 27% in NBC's and 22% approve of his handling of inflation in Fox's.
  • Even Republicans are souring: Fox and NBC both find Trump's approval among Republicans at 76%, while the Post puts it at 79%.

Zoom in: Republicans face a growing divide within their party.

  • Fox reports 95% approval of Trump among self-described MAGA Republicans, versus 47% among non-MAGA Republicans.
  • The Post finds 75% of MAGA Republicans say they're certain to vote or have already voted, compared with 57% of non-MAGA Republicans.
  • The Post poll also says 37% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents want GOP leaders to take the party in a different direction from Trump, an all-time high.

The big picture: A Reuters review published earlier this month found that Republican candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races either broke with Trump on policy or downplayed their ties to him.

  • At least a dozen of those candidates removed Trump's name, image or endorsement from their campaign websites, according to Reuters.
  • Even some Trump voters see the problem: A Politico poll found 26% of people who voted for Trump in 2024 believe Republican candidates would be better off breaking with him.

What they're saying: "Distancing yourself in general, that isn't anything new," Principles First executive director and Republican political strategist Brittany Martinez told Axios. "But Republicans, many Republicans, all over the country … intentionally, strategically" moving away from him "speaks volumes."

  • She noted some Republicans have criticized his policies without directly blaming him, pointing to an ad from Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) that warned Trump he should be careful about what his advisers were telling him about immigration policy.
  • Kentucky Senate nominee Andy Barr, Florida gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds and Georgia gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson are are among the candidates who removed references to Trump from their websites.

What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress."

  • Donalds' campaign comms director Gates McGavick said the congressman is "proud to have President Trump's endorsement."
  • A White House official told Axios there's no distance between Trump and candidates. Several candidates still sport their Trump ties front and center.

Between the lines: Republicans still appear with him, even if they don't always agree with his policies.

  • Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton has privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign. But he also appeared onstage with Trump at a campaign rally.
  • Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is also locked in a tight Senate race, called for an end to the war in Iran, citing high fuel prices for Iowans. Days later, she appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump and fellow lawmakers.

The bottom line: Republican candidates are trying to hold onto Trump's devoted base without letting his growing unpopularity define their campaigns.

item.title: Wright calls Trump's diesel deal a peace incentive. Rubio says Russia would sell anyway.
item.description:
President Trump's top aides offered sharply different explanations this weekend of his Russian diesel deal amid a barrage of bipartisan criticism calling the move a gift to Russia.

Why it matters: Oil, gas and petroleum products help finance Russia's war on Ukraine, and Trump's moves are bringing rifts within the GOP just ahead of midterm elections.

Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month.

  • That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans.

Driving the news: Energy Secretary Chris Wright argued Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that Russia could only benefit from the diesel deal if it scales back its war on Ukraine enough to increase exports.

  • "This is a carrot to try to end a war. It's not an economic lifeline for Russia," he said.
  • Yet Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a different explanation Saturday, saying Russia would have sold the diesel regardless of Trump's intervention.
  • "That diesel was going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, per a State Department transcript.

The diesel deal "is an incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week."

Context: Ukranian drone strikes against Russian refineries have dramatically hindered Russia's diesel exports.

  • Ukraine resumed those strikes after Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump's claim that the two sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire.
  • The combination of the Iran war — which has throttled supply and damaged Middle East refineries — and Russia's export decline have pushed up diesel costs.

Zoom out: The Sunday shows and Rubio's remarks provided the Trump team's most detailed comments on Friday night's executive order, which declines to use new powers under the law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

  • The move avoids putting fresh pressure on China and India, both major buyers of Russian oil.
  • Rubio said Trump wants time to "analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy."

Wright pointed to ongoing negotiations with China on trade and the war in Ukraine, stressing to CNN that Trump retains the power to impose the penalties later.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on NBC's "Meet the Press," defended the recent decisions by pointing to sanctions the administration imposed on Russian oil and gas giants Rosneft and Lukoil in 2025.
  • "No one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump," he said.

The other side: A number of Republicans have criticized the White House.

  • Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called the sanctions waiver "beyond irresponsible," while Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the late Lindsey Graham "would be appalled."
  • Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called the waiver a "mistake," and Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) said the U.S. should be increasing pressure on Russia and requested a classified briefing on the decision.

What we're watching: As the midterms hit their final frenzied weeks, Republicans have shown an increasing willingness to put distance between themselves and Trump.

item.title: Trump tells Axios why he endorsed Netanyahu's reelection
item.description:
President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, just nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 elections.

Why it matters: Trump's decision to weigh in nine days ahead of the election could give Netanyahu a boost at a critical moment in the Israeli leader's fight for political survival, with most polls showing his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

  • This is the first time in the history of the U.S.–Israel relations that a U.S. president explicitly and publicly endorsed a candidate in the Israeli elections.

What he is saying: In a Sunday post on Truth Social, Trump called Netanyahu "a Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "great partner" in the war against Iran.

  • "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote.
  • Trump called Netanyahu "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel" and gave him his "Complete and Total Endorsement."

Behind the scenes: Trump began planning his endorsement earlier this week.

  • "I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," Trump told Axios in a short phone interview on Sunday.
  • Trump said he endorsed Netanyahu because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected.
  • "It is important that Israel has a person they can count on," Trump said.
  • Asked if he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?"

The other side: Netanyahu thanked Trump for his endorsement in an X post.

  • "Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu wrote.
  • Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, told Israel's Channel 12 that he respects the U.S. president and appreciates what he has done for Israel.
  • "But the elections are a domestic Israeli issue. The only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel, and I will stand firm on this," Eisenkot said.

The big picture: Trump had repeatedly declined to endorse Netanyahu in recent months amid growing tensions between the two leaders over Iran and Gaza.

  • ⁠Some of Netanyahu's rivals urged Trump to remain neutral, Axios previously reported.
  • Some of Trump's closest advisers believed his Middle East agenda would fare better if Netanyahu lost and a different government formed.
  • Trump himself has been very frustrated with Netanyahu, including in recent weeks.
  • In private conversations, Trump blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failures to prevent the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks. Trump called the prime minister "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether Netanyahu was damaging Israel's international reputation, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president.
  • However, Trump decided to stick with Netanyahu.

Driving the news: Netanyahu and Trump discussed two weeks ago the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, Axios reported.

  • Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward accepting Netanyahu's proposal and resuming attacks, but he grew more hesitant and decided to wait until after the elections.
  • In his endorsement, Trump seemed to suggest he would let Netanyahu strike Iran after the midterm elections, saying "we will soon finish the job."

This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates

item.title: Trump once questioned Obama's citizenship. Now Obama is speaking out for Ilhan Omar.
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama issued a forceful denunciation of the Trump administration's legal pursuit of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar over suspicions she fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship decades ago, an allegation the Minnesota lawmaker has called "disgusting lies."

Why it matters: Obama — who faced false claims for years from Donald Trump that he wasn't an American citizen — is selective about when he weighs in on political issues or the president. His decision to speak out reflects his view that the DOJ raid on Omar's home last week was a betrayal of American values.

What he's saying: "The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar's political views," Obama wrote on X.

  • "Because if this becomes the new normal, there's no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

Driving the news: Federal agents raided Omar's Washington home Monday, seizing her phone as part of an investigation into whether she or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork 26 years ago.

  • The Wall Street Journal reported the administration aims to build "a case to strip her of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her."
  • Omar arrived in the U.S. from Somalia in 1995 as a child. She became a citizen through her father's naturalization in 2000 when records indicate she was 17.
  • But investigators are seeking evidence that she was a year older and therefore not automatically eligible for citizenship.

Flashback: The first Trump administration reviewed similar allegations in 2019, including questions about her birth date and her father's immigration, but found insufficient evidence to pursue a full investigation, the Washington Post reported.

  • The allegation gained attention through a viral claim on social media, according to the Post.

The other side: Omar has denounced the investigation as a witch hunt meant to intimidate one of Trump's fiercest critics in Congress.

  • Democrats have called it an abuse of power — especially just weeks before an election.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro also said her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, despite a congressional watchdog's recommendation last month to dismiss allegations of misconduct related to the filings.

Zoom in: Obama's more than 400-word statement was a full-throated denunciation of the Trump administration.

  • "Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it's not the first time this has happened," he wrote.
  • He added, "In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar's life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she's been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota."

item.title: Decades-old GOP winning streaks are suddenly at risk
item.description:
Democrats are running surprisingly competitive races in traditionally Republican territory across the country this midterm election cycle, and it's putting GOP winning streaks at risk that stretch as far back as the 1930s.

Why it matters: Democrats hope ending political droughts in states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina will help make inroads in what has long been off-limits territory.

Kansas - 1932

  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor who has significantly outraised the incumbent GOP senator.
  • The two are neck-and-neck in the polls, and Cook Political Report rates the race a tossup.
  • A Democrat hasn't won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas since George McGill was reelected in 1932.

Texas - 1988

  • Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is giving Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) a real run for his money in the Senate race. Talarico generally leads in polls by low single digits. Cook rates it a tossup.
  • Texas has been a consistent heartbreaker for Democrats in recent cycles. They last won a Senate seat in the state with Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

South Carolina - 1998

  • Polls have routinely shown Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham following his death in July, leading Democrat Annie Andrews by just a few percentage points.
  • Andrews, like other Democratic Senate candidates, has raised colossal sums, while Graham has struggled as a political neophyte. Still, Cook rates the race as "likely Republican."
  • The state has gone Republican in every U.S. Senate election since longtime Democrat Fritz Hollings was last reelected in 1998.

Between the lines: Democrat Troy Jackson, if he defeats Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine next month, would be the first registered Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Maine since 1988.

  • That's a bit of a technicality: Independent Sen. Angus King has caucused with Democrats since he was first elected in 2012.

Gubernatorial races

  • Texas hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990, but Democrat Gina Hinojosa is in a tight race with Republican incumbent Greg Abbott that Cook rates as "leans Republican."
  • Democrat David Jolly is also hoping for an upset against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds in a race Cook also rates as "leans Republican." Democrats narrowly won the Florida governorship in 1994 and have lost ever since.
  • Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms and Alaska's Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins are both vying to be the first Democrats elected governor in their states since 1998. Cook rates Georgia as a tossup and Alaska as "leans Democratic."

House races

  • Democrats have never won Nevada's 2nd District, which was created in 1983. It has changed shape over time but has always been anchored in the rural north half of the state.
  • Democrats feel they have a strong candidate in former state Assembly Majority Leader Teresa Benitez-Thompson and a weak opponent in former Air Force lieutenant colonel Dave Flippo.
  • The party is also bullish about Montana's 1st District, where they hope the populist appeal of former smokejumper Sam Forstag will help him prevail over the GOP nominee Aaron Flint, a veteran and radio host. Democrats haven't won a U.S. House seat in Montana since 1994.

Cook rates Nevada's 2nd Distric as "likely Republican" and Montana's 1st District as a tossup.

The other side: Republicans are also competitive in a handful of races where they haven't won in quite a while.

  • Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is locked in a tight U.S. Senate race in Michigan with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. He would be the first Republican elected to the Senate from the state since the 1994 GOP wave.
  • Democratic Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek faces a close race with Republican Christine Drazan, who would be the first Republican elected governor of the state since 1982.
  • Oregon is essentially the GOP's version of Texas: Republicans have lost by single digits in gubernatorial elections since 2002.

  • Democrats feel they have a strong candidate in former state Assembly Majority Leader Teresa Benitez-Thompson and a weak opponent in former Air Force lieutenant colonel Dave Flippo.
  • The party is also bullish about Montana's 1st District, where they hope the populist appeal of former smokejumper Sam Forstag will help him prevail over the GOP nominee Aaron Flint, a veteran and radio host. Democrats haven't won a U.S. House seat in Montana since 1994.

Cook rates Nevada's 2nd Distric as "likely Republican" and Montana's 1st District as a tossup.

The other side: Republicans are also competitive in a handful of races where they haven't won in quite a while.

  • Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is locked in a tight U.S. Senate race in Michigan with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. He would be the first Republican elected to the Senate from the state since the 1994 GOP wave.
  • Democratic Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek faces a close race with Republican Christine Drazan, who would be the first Republican elected governor of the state since 1982.
  • Oregon is essentially the GOP's version of Texas: Republicans have lost by single digits in gubernatorial elections since 2002.

item.title: Anti-party, anti-politician candidates surge in midterms
item.description:
In red states and blue, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or even disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington.

Why it matters: They might not all win, but the sheer number of political outsiders connecting with voters tells us something about the electorate: It's angry and willing to take risks.

  • The candidates — whether they come from the pulpit or the NFL sidelines — are making the same bet: Voters are tired of career politicians.

Zoom in: Consider three unorthodox Democrats leading in Senate contests in three red states: a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas (state Rep. James Talarico), a megachurch pastor in Kansas (Adam Hamilton), and an Alaska Native in that state (former Rep. Mary Peltola, who once skipped a week of House votes to go fishing when Chinook salmon were running).

  • Deep-blue Minnesota's Senate race features Michele Tafoya — a former NFL sideline reporter who's endorsed by President Trump but calls herself an independent Republican. She's mounting a serious challenge to Democrat Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor.
  • In House races, on the Democratic side there's a smokejumper in Montana (Sam Forstag), a 29-year-old barista in Colorado (Melat Kiros) and a Tejano singer in Texas (Bobby Pulido).

Four independent Senate candidates are courting Democratic voters without running with a (D) next to their names — and sometimes without a Democrat officially in the race.

  • In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, a union steamfitter and former factory mechanic, is mounting a serious independent challenge to Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former two-term governor whose family owns the Chicago Cubs.
  • In Montana, Seth Bodnar, a former Army Green Beret and University of Montana president, is running as an independent for an open Senate seat. Democrats tried to persuade their nominee to drop out, but she stayed in the race.
  • In South Dakota, Brian Bengs, a onetime park ranger, is challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds as an independent. Four years ago, Bengs ran against Sen. John Thune as a Democrat.
  • In Idaho, former Army tank commander and tech executive Todd Achilles is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Jim Risch. (Achilles previously served in the Idaho House as a Democrat. The official Democratic Senate nominee dropped out of the race in July.)

For many Republicans, quasi-Democrats running as independents amount to foul play — an attempt to deceive voters by discarding an unpopular brand.

Between the lines: Even candidates with more conventional backgrounds are shading their biographies to meet the populist moment.

  • In the Maine Senate race, Democrat Troy Jackson — who spent two decades in the state House and Senate before being term-limited out in 2024 — introduces himself as a fifth-generation Maine logger.

Zoom out: The populist path to Washington is at least as old as President Andrew Jackson, who first took office in 1829. It's as fresh as President Trump.

  • In recent years, there have been unorthodox candidates on both sides. Some succeeded; others didn't.
  • Al Franken, famous for being a writer and actor on "Saturday Night Live," won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota in 2008 and served more than eight years before resigning.
  • Herschel Walker, a celebrated college and NFL running back, couldn't find the end zone in his 2022 Senate race in Georgia.

Say what you want about the 45th and 47th president: The New York developer with a penchant for gold leaf has connected with disaffected working-class voters.

  • Democrats have struggled to match Trump's appeal to non-college-educated voters, but Trump has made their task easier this cycle with an unpopular war and tariffs that voters blame for high prices.

The bottom line: A version of the insurgent-vs.-establishment battle played out in Democratic primaries earlier this year, when seven House incumbents went down — tying a 21st-century high.

  • That included Kiros, the 29-year-old Colorado barista and democratic socialist who defeated a 15-term incumbent in the primary and is on a glide path to victory next month.

item.title: The overlooked geography of American poverty
item.description:
Data: U.S. Census; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data.

Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account.

  • Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture.

What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%.

  • The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average.
  • California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure, or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%.
  • Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%.

How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography.

  • The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs.

Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%.

  • Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate.
  • Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025.

Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate.

  • Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses.
  • The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller.

The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

item.title: Wanted: Chief small talk officers. Awkward applicants welcome
item.description:
Some people don't like to make small talk. Others — especially younger Americans— say they simply don't know how to do it.

Why it matters: A communication-skills app is betting that a baptism by fire in small talk can help rebuild social confidence — and it's hiring people to approach strangers to put that theory to the test.

Driving the news: RiseGuide is hiring Chief Small Talk Officers — recently rebranded from Head of Hanging Out to stress the seriousness of the assignment.

  • The monthlong gig pays each of up to three hires $2,000, plus a budget for outings to parks, bookstores and fitness classes, where they'll strike up conversations with strangers.
  • Officers will rate their small talk skills before and after the assignment, with regular check-ins to assess their interactions. They'll also track conversation lengths and strangers' receptiveness, Anastasia Sliusarenko, RiseGuide's brand and reputation manager, tells Axios.
  • "I'm personally rooting for applicants who kind of feel socially awkward," she says, because their improvement could be more noticeable. She acknowledges the irony of using an app to combat screen time, but says the ultimate goal is for users to "get off the app" and practice their skills in real life.

What they're saying: "We actually know from research that something like social confidence can actually be trained... it's not a personality trait," Laura Berssenbrugge, a therapist who specializes in working with Gen Z and Gen Alpha, tells Axios.

  • Social confidence doesn't have to look like the loudest extrovert in the room, Berssenbrugge adds. "That can be social confidence for them. Ours might look a little bit different, and that is absolutely okay."

The big picture: Smartphones and personalized digital feeds may be changing how Americans find common ground and navigate conversations with strangers.

  • Earlier generations often shared cultural reference points, from limited TV channels to major sporting events, that offered easy conversation starters. Today's algorithms instead feed people niche interests, reducing opportunities for common ground.
  • Phones also offer an easy escape from awkward interactions, potentially reducing opportunities to practice face-to-face conversation.

Zoom in: Even bars, once natural gathering places for spontaneous conversations, aren't immune to the shift, D.C.-area bartender Matty Pivec tells Axios.

  • "If you're sitting at a bar, you kind of naturally fall into place of talking to the person next to you... If you have your phone while you're waiting for the bartender, it's much easier to avoid that."
  • "It's become more of a chore than kind of a pleasant surprise to be able to hold a conversation with a stranger," he says, adding, "I think it's kind of a dying thing to go out and meet strangers."
  • John Lemay, a 14-year veteran bartender at D.C.-area bar Spider Kelly's, partly blames dating apps: "Why would you engage in conversation with somebody [at a bar] if you can just check those boxes and wham, your perfect date pops up," he says.

Between the lines: Avoiding strangers might spare people the anxiety of appearing awkward or "cringe," but it also cuts them off from the psychological benefits of casual interactions.

  • Psychologist Ellen Hendriksen points to a study of Chicago rush hour commuters that found those who interacted with strangers reported more positive experiences than those who kept to themselves.
  • Many "underestimated how much they were going to enjoy that," she says.

The bottom line: The goal isn't to become an extrovert. It's to get comfortable with the discomfort of striking up conversations with strangers.

Go deeper: Birding, silent book club, Mahjong and more: America's meetup explosion

item.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system still restricted in Ukraine
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk-owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs this week that it had been fully restored.

Why it matters: The current restrictions limit the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones and from using its drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines, Zelensky said.

The intrigue: Ukrainian officials say they are still scrambling to determine whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk.

  • Ukrainian officials have heard different versions of what happened, with the Trump administration and SpaceX executives accusing each other.
  • "SpaceX as a company tells us it is a technical problem. But our contacts in the company say it is coming from the White House. When we ask the White House, they say it is Elon," a Ukrainian official told Axios.

Musk said in a Wednesday X post that the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield.

  • "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
  • President Trump said on Friday that the White House was not involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system.

Behind the scenes: The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk proposed to Trump throttling the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military.

  • A source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn't push back on Elon's idea.
  • A White House official denied the Telegraph's account. "This is totally false. As President Trump said, we didn't slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational," the official said.

State of play: But the service is not fully operational. Before the restrictions, the Starlink and Starshield network operated even on drones that reached 400 kilometers per hour. Now it is restricted to 161 kilometers per hour, Ukrainian officials say.

  • Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that the Ukrainian military tested the system on Friday in cars in European Union countries.
  • The cars drove 180 kilometers per hour, and the satellite systems continued working. But once the cars crossed into Ukraine, the system disconnected at 161 kilometers per hour.
  • "The conclusion is that the restrictions apply inside Ukraine but do not apply in European Union countries. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelensky said.
  • Zelensky also expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems.

The other side: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday evening before leaving on a trip to India that he is "not sure Zelensky knows what he is talking about."

  • Rubio said nobody in the U.S. government ordered Starlink to be slowed down. "It sort of happened," Rubio said, adding the system "is back up and running."

Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded.

  • Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones.
  • The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes.
  • Ukraine said both systems were restricted.

What to watch: On Friday, Ukraine's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke with Trump's adviser and envoy, Jared Kushner, to discuss the Starlink issue, Zelensky said.

  • They also spoke about holding a meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian teams next week to continue the discussions on the latest Trump administration proposal for a deal with Russia on ending the war.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Secretary Rubio.

item.title: Trump's Russia waiver draws instant bipartisan backlash
item.description:
Top Republicans and Democrats alike lined up Saturday to condemn President Trump's decision to waive recent sanctions on Russia, calling it "irresponsible" and "a deal with the devil." Why it matters: Trump already faces a bipartisan effort to overturn his Russian diesel deal when Congress returns after the election.

  • Now he may have to deal with even broader outrage over sanctions Congress approved just a month ago.

Driving the news: Late Friday night, Trump issued an executive order waiving implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed in September.

  • The act would have imposed broad sanctions not only on Russia, but on other countries buying its oil.

What they're saying: Democrats forcefully criticized Trump's decision.

  • "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote.
  • "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X.
  • "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X.

Republicans were equally unsparing.

  • "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote. "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision."
  • "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."
  • Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled."

Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision.

  • "The president and I share the same goal to end the war, get gas and diesel prices down, and the [Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act] bill is one of the tools he can use to do that," she said, adding that it was up to Trump if he uses it or not.
  • "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia ... because I don't trust Putin."

One soon-to-depart congressman, Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns.

  • "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote.

For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision.

  • "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
  • "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."

What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.

  • "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X.
  • "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X.

Republicans were equally unsparing.

  • "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote. "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision."
  • "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."
  • Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled."

Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision.

  • "The president and I share the same goal to end the war, get gas and diesel prices down, and the [Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act] bill is one of the tools he can use to do that," she said, adding that it was up to Trump if he uses it or not.
  • "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia ... because I don't trust Putin."

One soon-to-depart congressman, Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns.

  • "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote.

For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision.

  • "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
  • "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."

What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.
