item.title: New inflation warning sign
item.description:
America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy.

Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further.

What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note.

  • The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote.

By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month.

  • Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices.
  • Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.

The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening.

  • Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge.
  • Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs.
  • "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months.

The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December.

  • The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report.
  • Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch.

What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike.

  • But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated.
  • Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component."
  • Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures.

The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated.

  • The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months.
  • Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

item.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
item.description:
Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment.

Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter.

  • That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month.
  • The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax.

How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment.

Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January.

  • However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years.
  • The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

item.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said.

  • That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August.
  • Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month.

Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices.

  • Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August.
  • Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month.

Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country.

  • President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies.
  • Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices.

What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday.

  • The increase will take effect in January.

The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again, with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation.

  • In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices.
  • Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month.
  • New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027.

The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month.

  • Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.
item.content:encoded:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said.

  • That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August.
  • Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month.

Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices.

  • Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August.
  • Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month.

Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country.

  • President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies.
  • Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices.

What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday.

item.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
item.description:
Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a ... smart display?

Why it matters: Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future.

  • It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday.

Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts.

  • Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices.
  • "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios.

Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners.

  • HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4.
  • Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri.

The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets.

  • Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making.
  • Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm, a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses.

Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand.

  • U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana.
  • "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon.

Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones.

  • Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it's unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market.
  • "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios.

The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

item.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
item.description:
Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond.

Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action.

  • U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study.

Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat.

  • Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap."
  • The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next.
  • "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study.

State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models.

  • Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here."

Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions.

  • The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings.
  • Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans.

Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes.

  • Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions.
  • She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning.
  • One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a Ph.D. student in Cornell's Information Science Department.

What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions.

  • AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said.
  • That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said.

The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

item.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
item.description:
President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions.

Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters.

Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots.

  • On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues.
  • On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader.
  • On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington.
  • On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets.
  • On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary."

Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes.

  • For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war.
  • For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment, as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.
  • For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll.

The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton.

  • From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit, Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment.
  • A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus.

What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky."

  • "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas.

  • But as polling alarms pile up, the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power.
  • In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

item.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
item.description:
Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows.

Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work.

  • The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic.

Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios.

  • That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt.
  • It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker-backed AI safety group that has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4).

The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike.

  • OpenAI president Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI.
  • Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void.

Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future.

  • Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, when crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates.
  • "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said.

Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation.

  • Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology.

The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans.

  • In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action."

What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance executive director Shaunna Thomas said.

  • "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into — boldly."

Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI.

The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

item.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
item.description:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced.

Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected.

  • "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia.

The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington.

In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online.

  • "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded, referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer.
  • Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
  • "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back, pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course.

In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state.

  • Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects.
  • Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage.
  • In his closing statement, Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger."

In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge, as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points.

  • Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel, saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine.
  • Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war.
  • Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

item.title: Judge orders White House to reinstate press access until litigation concludes
item.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled the Trump administration must continue to grant CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds while the lawsuit filed by the three news organizations continues.

Why it matters: It marks a major win for the news outlets as it maintains their White House access and signals that the judge believes their legal claims could succeed on their merits.

  • Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, awarded a temporary restraining order to the plaintiffs on Sept. 24 that mandated the White House reinstate the outlets' credentials for 14 days. Last week, Kelly extended that through Oct. 13.
  • The preliminary injunction preserves the outlets' access until the case is resolved, which could take weeks, months or years.

Zoom in: "Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them [to] immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked on or about September 18, 2026," Kelly's court order said.

What they're saying: In a statement, Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, said the ban "blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment."

  • "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," he said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future."

Yes, but: The judge's ruling doesn't guarantee that the plaintiffs have access to key areas, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.

  • The White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico journalists from press pool assignments onboard Air Force One, despite the temporary restraining order reinstating their credentials.
  • A different White House lawsuit, brought by the Associated Press, could help clarify the extent of the president's power to bar reporters from those types of spaces. That case is ongoing.

Catch up quick: The news outlets sued the White House, arguing it violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints.

  • They also argued their Fifth Amendment rights were violated as they were banned without due process.
  • The temporary restraining order and the preliminary injunction suggest the judge believes the plaintiffs have a strong case on the Fifth Amendment claims.
  • Further legal proceedings, including a potential trial, would determine whether the White House violated the outlets' First Amendment rights.

Reality check: Legal experts believe the news organizations have a strong case because of a precedent set by the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight case in which an appeals court ruled it was unconstitutional for the White House to arbitrarily revoke press credentials based on a journalist's reporting or viewpoint.

  • They point to comments President Trump made to justify the ban, including, "They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration."

What to watch: The broader White House press pool, which consists of outlets that cover the president and travel with him on rotation, has stood in solidarity with the barred outlets.

  • The White House reached out to other outlets to fill CNN and Politico's spots in the press pool, but they have refused.
  • Some outlets have indicated that they intend to continue withholding publication or distribution of images captured as part of the White House still photography pool, "until a court has the chance to hear arguments on the legal claims filed by those media organizations."

Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

Editor's note: This story was updated to include a statement from an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

item.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years.

Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research.

  • In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%.
  • That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis, a leading authority on Latino voting behavior.

Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP.

  • In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown.
  • The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters.
  • Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys.

Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living.

  • 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue.
  • 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans.
  • That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February.

The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress.

Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally.

  • The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.

item.title: Democrats fear "more October surprises" after "bullshit" raid on Ilhan Omar's home
item.description:
Congressional Democrats' private text chains lit up with fear and anger on Monday after Department of Homeland Security agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home in Washington, D.C.

Why it matters: The search came less than a month before the midterms, immediately setting off alarm bells among Democrats that "more October surprises" could be coming, as one senior Democrat told Axios.

  • Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) told Axios: "We expect more of this kind of thing."

Driving the news: Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" on Omar's home as part of an ongoing immigration probe, the Justice Department said in a statement.

  • DOJ has not detailed the scope or subject of the search warrant.
  • Fox News reported the investigation concerns Omar's immigration paperwork. She came to the United States in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee from Somalia.
  • Omar's office and Democratic House leadership quickly denounced the action as an "abuse of power," with a spokesperson for Omar saying she "has done nothing wrong."

What we're hearing: "People are outraged. ... [This is] what authoritarian tyrants and dictators do," said the senior House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay colleagues' private conversations.

  • Another House Democrat told Axios "the chatter on texts" is that "folks are irate."

Zoom out: Democrats allege the raid fits into a broader pattern of Trump using federal resources to boost Republicans and target his political opponents.

  • DHS became embroiled in controversy just last week after a statement targeting Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson, which critics said violates federal laws restricting partisan activities by federal officials.
  • Trump has also come under fire for using taxpayer funds to run campaign-style television ads touting him and his administration in the run-up to the midterms.

What they're saying: "President Trump will keep trying to intimidate and bully Americans ahead of the midterms," said Balint, adding, "We suspect he will try anything to stay in power and in control."

  • Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) said that "of course there will" be more like the Omar raid, saying Trump is "the pettiest, worst human being" and "can't help himself."
  • Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios: "This is some serious hate-baiting bullshit. This administration is just despicable."
  • Asked whether he expects more, Huffman said, "Of course."

The other side: One congressional Republican cheered the raid on Omar, who has long been the target of right-wing attacks on her immigration status.

  • "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and deported," Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) wrote in a post on X, also comparing Monday's raid to the 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago.
  • The White House, DOJ and DHS did not respond to a request for comment.

What to watch: House Democratic leaders are already signaling plans to wrap this into their oversight agenda if they retake the majority.

  • "We will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his deputies said in a statement.
  • House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said in a statement: "We will be demanding transparency and accountability as to who authorized this abusive search and who carried it out."

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
item.description:
The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program.

Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history.

What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release.

The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering.

Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions.

  • Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late.
  • More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said.

Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history.

  • Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran.

Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted.

  • Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity.

The other side: In a statement, Bank of America said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime.

  • "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."

What to watch: Bank of America reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in those results.

  • The bank said costs associated with its ongoing efforts to fix compliance problems are already reflected in its expenses.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar under investigation by Jeanine Pirro's office
item.description:
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home.

The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked."

Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well."

  • "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe.

Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported.

  • Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."
  • Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country."

Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures.

  • A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million.
  • She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors.
  • Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's request for comment.

What they're saying: After Pirro's appearance on Fox News, Trump shared a post on Truth Social suggesting, without evidence, that Omar benefited from fraud in Minnesota.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
item.description:
Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.

What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday.

  • The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect.

Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery.

  • "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said.
  • The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement.

Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center.

  • It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things.
  • Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer.

The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups.

  • Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized."
  • He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers.

Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung

Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about Leo's diagnosis.

item.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter.

  • Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official.
  • The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms.

Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later.

  • But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said.
  • "Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said.
  • A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said.
  • Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations."

Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran.

  • According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets.
  • Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program.
  • Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site.
  • Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes.

Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant.

  • A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue.
  • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said.
  • But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now.
  • "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said.

Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders.

  • Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation.
  • Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call.
  • Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said.
  • Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment.
  • It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical.

The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said.

  • In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join.
  • Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher.

The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions.

  • "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said.
  • "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added.
  • Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

item.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States.

Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny, with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen.

Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting, will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed.

  • Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement, Axios' Marc Caputo reported.
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired.

Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center..

  • The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR.
  • The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett.

How a firing squad works

State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves.

How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood.

  • A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head.

The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner.

  • If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss.

Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method.

  • For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition.
  • Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood.

Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart.

Where firing squad is legal

The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC.

  • It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer.
  • The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection.

Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions.

Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

What we know about the execution livestream

Few specifics are known about the livestream execution, where it would streamed, or how people would watch it.

  • It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood.
  • It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies.

What we're watching: The Army.

  • Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.
